group.title: Emotions in depth
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Extremely upset and shocked by something terrible.
examples: She was {devastated} when her dog died.
wrong: He was devastated to hear the wonderful news.

words.meaning: Having so many feelings or tasks that you cannot cope.
examples: I felt {overwhelmed} by all the kind messages.
wrong: She was overwhelmed because she had nothing at all to do.

words.meaning: Very happy and excited about something.
examples: The team was {elated} after winning the final.
wrong: He was elated after failing every one of his exams.

words.meaning: Extremely happy, full of strong joy.
examples: The fans were {ecstatic} when the band came on stage.
wrong: She was ecstatic, so she sat in the corner and cried with sadness.

words.meaning: Feeling angry because you think you were treated unfairly.
examples: He felt {resentful} that his brother got all the attention.
wrong: She felt resentful because everyone treated her so fairly.

words.meaning: An angry feeling about unfair treatment that lasts a long time.
examples: Years of {resentment} came out during the argument.
wrong: Her resentment showed in how warmly she thanked him.

words.meaning: Wanting something that another person has.
examples: I’m {envious} of your long summer holiday.
wrong: He was envious of her, so he was glad he had nothing she had.

words.meaning: An unhappy feeling of wanting what someone else has, or of fearing to lose someone’s love.
examples: His {jealousy} grew when she started spending time with new friends.
wrong: Her jealousy made her truly happy for her rival’s success.

words.meaning: Slightly worried that something bad may happen.
examples: She was {apprehensive} about her first day at the new job.
wrong: He was apprehensive, so he felt completely calm and sure.

words.meaning: To feel very worried about something that is going to happen.
examples: I {dread} going to the dentist.
wrong: I dread my birthday party because I am so looking forward to it.

words.meaning: A good feeling when a worry or pain ends.
examples: It was a huge {relief} to hear that everyone was safe.
wrong: To her relief, the bad news made her even more worried.

words.meaning: The feeling of being thankful.
examples: He wrote a letter to express his {gratitude} to the nurses.
wrong: She showed her gratitude by ignoring the person who helped her.

words.meaning: Feeling happy and a little sad when thinking about the past.
examples: Old photos always make me feel {nostalgic}.
wrong: He felt nostalgic about tomorrow’s meeting.

words.meaning: A calm feeling of being happy with what you have.
examples: She smiled with quiet {contentment} as she looked at her garden.
wrong: His contentment made him complain about everything he owned.

words.meaning: Deep sadness, especially after someone dies.
examples: Her {grief} after her father’s death lasted for months.
wrong: His grief at the party made him dance and laugh all night.

words.meaning: A feeling of great sadness.
examples: The town shared its {sorrow} at the loss of the old teacher.
wrong: She was full of sorrow because it was the best day of her life.

words.meaning: The feeling of having lost all hope.
examples: In {despair}, he gave up looking for his lost ring.
wrong: In despair, she was sure everything would turn out fine.

words.meaning: Feeling that nothing good can happen or that things cannot improve.
examples: After the third rejection, he felt {hopeless}.
wrong: She felt hopeless, so she was full of confidence for the future.

words.meaning: Easily annoyed or made angry.
examples: I get {irritable} when I’m hungry.
wrong: He is so irritable that nothing ever bothers him.

words.meaning: Annoyed and bored with something that has gone on too long.
examples: I’m {fed up} with this rain.
wrong: She was fed up with the trip, so she wanted it to go on forever.

words.meaning: Feeling bad because you did something wrong.
examples: He was {ashamed} of lying to his parents.
wrong: She was ashamed of her kind act and proud of it.

words.meaning: A bad feeling that you did something wrong.
examples: She felt {guilt} for forgetting her friend’s birthday.
wrong: He felt guilt about something he had done perfectly well.

words.meaning: Deep regret for something wrong you have done.
examples: The driver showed real {remorse} for the accident.
wrong: He felt remorse for the good deed he was proud of.

words.meaning: Made to feel ashamed and foolish in front of others.
examples: He felt {humiliated} when he fell on stage.
wrong: She was humiliated when everyone praised her speech.

words.meaning: Very pleased and excited.
examples: We’re {thrilled} that you can come to the wedding.
wrong: I’m thrilled about the news, so I feel really disappointed.

words.meaning: Full of excited, lively energy.
examples: She felt {exhilarated} after the roller coaster ride.
wrong: The fast ride left him exhilarated and bored.

words.meaning: Strong care for people who are suffering and a wish to help them.
examples: The nurse treated every patient with {compassion}.
wrong: He showed compassion by laughing at the injured man.

words.meaning: A gentle feeling of love and liking.
examples: She looked at her grandson with great {affection}.
wrong: He showed his affection by refusing to speak to her.

words.meaning: Very confused and unable to understand.
examples: The tourists looked {bewildered} by the subway map.
wrong: She was bewildered, so she understood everything clearly.

words.meaning: Suddenly surprised or a little frightened.
examples: The {startled} cat jumped off the table.
wrong: He was startled by the noise he had expected for hours.

words.meaning: Extremely afraid.
examples: She is {terrified} of spiders.
wrong: He was terrified, so he walked calmly up to the lion.

words.meaning: Very sad, especially after losing someone you love.
examples: He was {heartbroken} when his girlfriend left him.
wrong: She was heartbroken about the wonderful surprise.

words.meaning: Worried about how you look or what others think of you.
examples: He felt {self-conscious} about his new haircut.
wrong: She was so self-conscious that she never cared what anyone thought.

words.meaning: Very strong anger about something unfair or shocking.
examples: The decision caused public {outrage}.
wrong: Their outrage showed how pleased they were with the plan.

words.meaning: Angry because you think something is unfair.
examples: She was {indignant} at being blamed for his mistake.
wrong: He was indignant because he was treated so fairly.

words.meaning: Unable to stay still or relax because you are bored or worried.
examples: The children grew {restless} during the long speech.
wrong: He was restless, so he sat perfectly still for hours.

words.meaning: A sudden change from one feeling to a very different one.
examples: Lack of sleep can cause {mood swings}.
wrong: His mood swing kept him feeling the same all week.

words.meaning: Nervous and unable to relax.
examples: Everyone was {on edge} waiting for the results.
wrong: She was on edge, totally relaxed and sleepy.

words.meaning: Extremely happy.
examples: She has been {on cloud nine} since the wedding.
wrong: He was on cloud nine after hearing the terrible news.

words.meaning: To suddenly start crying.
examples: When she heard the news, she {burst into tears}.
wrong: He burst into tears and stayed completely dry-eyed.
